This page corresponds to the exact occupation O*NET/SOC 49-3042.00 "Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanics, Except Engines" (Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanics): diagnose, adjust, repair, or overhaul mobile mechanical, hydraulic, and pneumatic equipment used in construction, logging, and mining, such as cranes, bulldozers, graders, and conveyors. Official scope text: Diagnose, adjust, repair, or overhaul mobile mechanical, hydraulic, and pneumatic equipment, such as cranes, bulldozers, graders, and conveyors, used in construction, logging, and mining. The core tasks listed by O*NET include: repairing and replacing damaged or worn parts; testing mechanical products and equipment after repair or assembly to ensure proper performance and conformity with manufacturer specifications; operating and inspecting machines or heavy equipment to diagnose defects; reading and understanding operating manuals and drawings and technical diagrams; disassembling and reassembling heavy equipment using rigging and hand tools; and overhauling and testing machines. Common job titles include Heavy Equipment Mechanic and Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanic and Construction Equipment Mechanic and Field Service Technician and Heavy Equipment Technician. Scope note: the U.S. wage and employment data presented by O*NET on the 49-3042.00 page are not marked as taken from a parent or adjacent occupation, and this page labels them faithfully according to this occupation's (49-3042.00) own scope; this occupation in the United States is Job Zone Three (medium preparation required) (6.0 to less than 7.0 (SVP 6.0 to < 7.0)) and is marked Bright Outlook; this page does not extrapolate the U.S. scope to mainland China's job titles, qualifications, or wages.

Practice prompt | a completely fictitious mobile heavy equipment repair task package (for practicing the process only, and not representing any real company, customer, or data). Please write a draft plan: (1) how to arrange a diagnosis and repair or overhaul in a structured way based on a fictitious fault repair request and equipment materials (equipment type and model and operating conditions, fault symptoms and operator description, hydraulic and pneumatic and electrical and mechanical systems, diagnostic steps and tests, needed tools and spare parts, repair or overhaul plan, assembly and testing and acceptance, downtime and schedule and handover), and state which information is insufficient and needs to be supplemented (equipment history and repair records, site conditions and support and lifting conditions, safety and access requirements, spare parts supply and schedule); (2) how to design filling-in and review points for a fictitious repair and inspection record form (fields and definitions, equipment and work order identifiers, faults and diagnosis, disassembly and replacement and assembly, test and acceptance data, anomalies and rework and outstanding items, original records and revision trail); (3) how to write a handover-ready repair summary (equipment — symptoms and diagnosis — disposition — testing and acceptance — outstanding items and recommendations); (4) how to record and retain equipment and repair and customer data, and distinguish publicly shareable information from controlled materials or materials involving customer and manufacturer technical data; (5) how to pause and review and isolate and report when a hydraulic or electrical or lifting or confined space risk, or going beyond job authorization or a safety risk is found. Use public materials and simulated data to answer, and do not use any real company or customer data.

Fit signals | The work activity importance for U.S. O*NET 49-3042.00 shows: repairing and maintaining mechanical equipment (88) and operating vehicles, mechanized devices, or equipment (86) and inspecting equipment, structures, or materials (85) and making decisions and solving problems (83) and obtaining information (81) and identifying objects, actions, and events (78) and communicating with supervisors, peers, or subordinates (77) are this occupation's most important activities; the work context shows: exposure to hazardous equipment and heavy machinery is common, exposure to oil and grime and dust and exhaust is common, exposure to noise is common, serious consequences of error (equipment damage and personal injury), high precision and diagnostic accuracy requirements, and constraints from downtime and project schedules. If you are willing to work with your hands on equipment fault diagnosis and disassembly and repair, can read drawings and manuals and do testing and assembly and acceptance solidly, and take responsibility for equipment and personal safety and repair quality, this occupation's daily requirements are closer to your way of working.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows (49-3042.00, work context and task scope): exposure to hazardous equipment and heavy machinery is common; exposure to oil and grime and dust and exhaust is common; working under equipment and in narrow spaces is common; often outdoors and in workshops and exposed to extremely hot or extremely cold temperatures; serious consequences of error (equipment damage and personal injury); high responsibility for others' health and safety; and constraints from downtime and project schedules. This occupation deals with heavy mobile equipment and hydraulic and pneumatic and electrical and mechanical systems: one improper handling of a high-pressure hydraulic or pneumatic system, one improper lifting or support, one hot work or electrical work mistake, or one inadequate diagnosis or repair or assembly leading to a recurring fault can all cause equipment damage, personal injury, downtime losses, and compliance risk. O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone Three (medium preparation required) (6.0 to less than 7.0 (SVP 6.0 to < 7.0)); the education section on that page shows 55% requiring a post-secondary certificate, 30% a high school diploma or equivalent, and 8% some college courses but no degree (the page does not account for the remaining 7%); and it is marked Bright Outlook. If you find it hard to work in oily and dusty and noisy and confined and outdoor environments, find it hard to accept a rhythm that changes with equipment downtime and project schedules and possible overtime, or are unwilling to take responsibility for safety and repair quality judgments, you should treat these as real costs.

Taking on judgment | Real fit comes from whether you can do three things at the same time on one repair task: do the technical work solidly (complete diagnosis and repair or overhaul and assembly and acceptance based on equipment and drawings and manuals and tests, producing usable repair and inspection records), keep safety and compliance and boundaries under control (work and keep records according to lifting and support and hot work and electrical and confined space and work permit requirements, distinguish publicly shareable information from controlled materials or materials involving customer and manufacturer technical data and handle them according to policy, and do not perform hot work or lifting or out-of-bounds handling without the required qualifications), and take on definable job responsibility (be responsible for your own diagnosis and repair and overhaul and assembly and acceptance and records, and refer matters beyond job authorization or involving special equipment and major safety matters to the appropriate position or organization according to policy). It is suggested to test this with one verifiable experience (completing a diagnosis and repair plan and an explanation of repair and inspection records for a fictitious repair request, or a review of handling a hydraulic leak or lifting or electrical anomaly), rather than relying only on the conclusion of an interest questionnaire.

Direct answer | The "Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanics" on this page is the exact occupation O*NET 49-3042.00 (Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanics, Except Engines), and the work can be divided into several categories: first, diagnosis and inspection — operating and inspecting equipment to diagnose defects, reading manuals and drawings and diagrams, and using diagnostic equipment and measuring tools to judge faults; second, repair and replacement — repairing or replacing damaged or worn parts, repairing electrical systems, welding or brazing damaged parts, and installing bearings; third, overhaul and assembly — disassembling and reassembling equipment using rigging and hand tools, adjusting or maintaining or repairing subassemblies, and assembling gear systems; fourth, testing and acceptance — testing equipment after repair or assembly to ensure proper performance and conformity with manufacturer specifications; fifth, maintenance and records — arranging maintenance and cleaning and lubrication and spare parts management, and recording repairs and tests and anomalies.

O*NET and BLS occupational profile highlights | This page corresponds to the exact occupation O*NET/SOC 49-3042.00 "Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanics, Except Engines" (Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanics), official scope text: Diagnose, adjust, repair, or overhaul mobile mechanical, hydraulic, and pneumatic equipment, such as cranes, bulldozers, graders, and conveyors, used in construction, logging, and mining. That page's work activity importance: repairing and maintaining mechanical equipment (91), operating vehicles, mechanized devices, or equipment (86), inspecting equipment, structures, or materials (85), making decisions and solving problems (81), obtaining information (79). The education section on that page shows 55% requiring a post-secondary certificate, 30% a high school diploma or equivalent, and 8% some college courses but no degree (the page does not account for the remaining 7%), and it is marked Bright Outlook.

Mainland China has not established a national occupational wage distribution precisely corresponding to this occupation, and this page registers the gap according to the evidence policy rather than filling it in.

Mainland China scope and gaps | Mainland China has positions in the construction machinery and heavy equipment repair field similar to Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanics (such as construction machinery repair worker, heavy equipment repair technician, equipment repair worker, and hydraulic and electrical repair personnel), and their work and lifting and hot work and working at height and confined space and safety and occupational health and records are governed by the Work Safety Law of the People's Republic of China and related regulations and standards on special operations and occupational health and environmental protection and metrology. However, the National Bureau of Statistics publishes average wages of urban unit employees by industry category and does not distinguish occupations, and public occupational statistics have not established a national occupational wage distribution precisely corresponding to O*NET 49-3042.00 (Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanics); this page retains the search scope and the gap, and does not infer starting pay, take-home income, or personal quotations from industry averages, recruitment offers, or U.S. data.

Safety and compliance notes | Organize work according to work safety and lifting and hot work and electrical and confined space and occupational health and record requirements: diagnosis and repair and testing and disassembly must be consistent with manuals and procedures and current standards and must indicate sources and limitations, and must not replace special equipment inspection, accident determinations, or safety permit requirements; operations involving lifting and hot work and working at height and confined space and electrical work must be handled with work permits and personal protection as required; the collection and use and external provision of customer and manufacturer technical materials and drawings and data must have a lawful basis, be limited to the minimum necessary scope, and be approved and documented according to policy.

The BLS 49-3042 projection for 2025—2035 is about 180,300 → 192,500 people, growth 6.7%, average annual openings 15,000 including replacements, and self-employment in the base period 1.8%; employment includes self-employment, and this is not real-time hiring, net new jobs, or AI causality.

Fault repair request checking → Operating and inspecting equipment and diagnosis → Disassembly and repair or replacement and overhaul → Assembly and adjustment and subassemblies → Testing and acceptance → Maintenance and spare parts and records and handover

Standards and quality boundaries | This page involves three types of requirements: first, technical and quality — diagnosis and repair and overhaul and assembly and testing must be performed according to manuals and drawings and manufacturer specifications with repair and inspection records kept; second, safety and occupational health — lifting and support and hot work and electrical and confined space and personal protection must meet work safety and special operations and occupational health requirements; third, environment and metrology — waste oil and grime and waste disposal and noise and metrology calibration must meet environmental protection and metrology requirements; all three are governed by the currently effective version and the requirements of the competent authority and the enterprise.

Records and collaboration | According to the enterprise's equipment and repair and quality management systems, record repair requests and work orders, on-site inspection and diagnosis and testing, disassembly and repair or replacement, assembly and adjustment and subassemblies, performance testing and acceptance, spare parts and inventory, anomalies and rework and outstanding items and handover and original records and revision trail, and check pending and completed equipment with operators and supervisors and suppliers; anomalies must be isolated and reported promptly.

Boundary conclusion | This page corresponds to O*NET 49-3042.00 (Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanics), and the core difference from adjacent positions lies in "subject matter and outputs and authorization level": this occupation takes the mobile heavy machinery and hydraulic and pneumatic and electrical systems used in construction and logging and mining as its subject matter, produces equipment diagnosed and repaired and overhauled and tested and conforming to manufacturer specifications together with traceable repair and inspection records, completes work and judgments within the scope of qualifications and job authorization based on mechanical and hydraulic and electrical and diagnostic ability, and is responsible for equipment and personal safety and repair quality; operators take equipment operation as the subject matter, diesel engine specialists take engines as the subject matter, and crane operators take lifting operations as the subject matter, with different responsibility and authorization levels.

Core concept of adjacent positions | Most positions in the same group and adjacent positions aim to "maintain or operate machinery or systems to the specified state within equipment and safety and quality requirements and keep records", with differences in subject matter and outputs and authorization level: some take the repair and overhaul of heavy mobile equipment as the subject matter, and some take operation or engines or lifting or farm equipment as the subject matter.

Core purpose of this occupation | Taking mobile heavy machinery and hydraulic and pneumatic and electrical systems and drawings and manuals and manufacturer specifications as the subject matter, complete work within the scope of qualifications and safety and authorization: diagnosis and inspection, repair and replacement, overhaul and assembly, testing and acceptance, maintenance and spare parts and records, producing equipment conforming to specifications and traceable records.

Main subject matter and basis of adjacent positions | Building construction machinery operators rely on equipment operation and construction procedures; surface mining excavating and loading machine operators rely on mining equipment operating procedures; bus and truck mechanics and diesel engine specialists rely on vehicle and engine repair specifications; farm equipment mechanics rely on agricultural machinery repair and technical specifications; crane and tower crane operators rely on lifting operation procedures. Most of them take operation or engines or farm machinery or lifting as the subject matter, which differs from this occupation's repair and overhaul of mobile heavy equipment.

Main subject matter and basis of this occupation | Taking equipment type and model and operating conditions, fault symptoms and diagnosis, hydraulic and pneumatic and electrical and mechanical systems, drawings and manuals and manufacturer specifications, tools and spare parts, repair and overhaul and assembly processes, testing and acceptance requirements, and safety and lifting and hot work and metrology requirements as the subject matter, complete work and judgments according to repair manuals and manufacturer specifications and work safety and occupational health and metrology requirements.

Occupational profile | The Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanics on this page is the exact occupation O*NET 49-3042.00 (Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanics, Except Engines), and takes on diagnosis and repair and overhaul tasks for mobile heavy equipment in equipment repair positions at construction and mining and logging and equipment rental and wholesale trade enterprises; the work is mainly on-site and workshop diagnosis and disassembly and repair and testing, accompanied by operation and inspection and records and collaboration, often performed in oily and dusty and noisy and confined and outdoor environments, and organized according to equipment downtime and project schedules.

Core processes of adjacent positions | Operators focus on operation and construction; diesel engine specialists focus on engine diagnosis and repair; farm equipment mechanics focus on agricultural machinery repair; crane operators focus on lifting operations; this occupation focuses on diagnosis and repair and overhaul and assembly and testing of mobile heavy equipment.

Core processes of this occupation | Accepting the repair request and checking materials, on-site inspection and diagnosis and testing, disassembly and repair or replacement and overhaul, assembly and adjustment and subassemblies, performance testing and acceptance, records and spare parts and handover; each step must be performed according to manuals and procedures and be reviewable by quality control and supervisors and operators.

Main outputs of adjacent positions | Operators produce construction work and equipment operation records; diesel engine specialists produce vehicle and engine repair records; farm equipment mechanics produce agricultural machinery repair records; crane operators produce lifting operation records; these differ from this occupation's mobile heavy equipment repair and inspection records.

Main outputs of this occupation | Equipment diagnosed and repaired and overhauled and assembled and passing performance testing and conforming to manufacturer specifications, repair and inspection and test records, spare parts and inventory and maintenance records, anomaly and rework and outstanding item records, and traceable work order and handover records.

Responsible parties of adjacent positions | Responsibility for positions in the same group and adjacent positions is usually defined by the affiliated enterprise and equipment and safety and quality systems, and the objects of responsibility are mostly equipment and personal safety and production continuity.

This occupation is responsible for the diagnosis and repair and overhaul and assembly and testing and records it personally performs, and for the work performed according to manuals and procedures and qualification requirements; matters involving special equipment inspection, lifting and hot work and electrical and major safety matters must be referred to the appropriate position or organization according to qualifications and job authorization and policy.

Authority and approval of adjacent positions | The authority of positions in the same group and adjacent positions comes from enterprise authorization and equipment and safety and professional specifications, and usually does not include the authority to decide on design changes or major dispositions beyond one's own authorization or scope; matters involving equipment modification and special equipment and major repair and safety matters should be transferred to the appropriate position or organization.

Authority and approval of this occupation | Daily diagnosis and repair and overhaul and assembly and testing must be carried out within the scope of qualifications and job authorization and manuals and procedures; matters involving special equipment inspection, lifting and hot work and electrical and confined space operations, and equipment modification and major repair must be carried out according to policy and qualifications; matters involving welding and lifting and electrical qualifications and work permits are governed by the requirements of the competent authority and the enterprise.

Conclusion boundaries of adjacent positions | Conclusions of positions in the same group and adjacent positions are mostly limited to this equipment or this process level and usually do not constitute a determination of the equipment's final safety or compliance or legal liability; conclusions that cross disciplines or involve special equipment and major safety have limits on their applicability.

Conclusion boundaries of this occupation | Diagnosis and repair and testing and acceptance conclusions state only verifiable test data and repair content and results, and distinguish measured facts from judgment inferences and items to be verified; conclusions on matters beyond one's own qualifications (special equipment inspection conclusions, accident determinations, final equipment acceptance) must not be issued in one's own name.

Pre-onboarding checklist notes | The following six items are used to check off one by one before applying and onboarding, to avoid inferring actual duties and authorization from the job title or promotional language; the check results should be based on written recruitment information and the employment contract and job description and equipment and safety system documents, and should be continuously confirmed after onboarding. This page only lists checklist points and does not constitute a hiring or safety conclusion.

Checklist point notes | Job titles are similar but duties and authorization differ greatly: some focus on field service and diagnosis, some on workshop overhaul and assembly, some on specific equipment (construction machinery or mining equipment or farm machinery or lifting equipment), and some also cover electrical and hydraulic systems; different enterprises and jurisdictions have different requirements for special operations and qualifications and safety, so check first and then judge fit.

01 Actual job duties and equipment and site authority | Check whether you truly take on independent diagnosis and repair and overhaul work, or mainly disassembly and assistance and cleaning; check the equipment types and systems you can repair (hydraulic and pneumatic and electrical and mechanical), the authority over tools and diagnostic equipment and spare parts, the authority to adjust equipment parameters and settings, and the interface relationships with operators and supervisors and suppliers.

Checklist point notes | This occupation often works in oily and dusty and noisy and confined and outdoor environments, and usually requires training in safety and lifting and support and hot work and electrical and confined space and work permits, and compliance with personal protection and emergency response requirements.

02 Safety and occupational health and lifting and hot work requirements | Check whether the enterprise requires and provides: safety operating procedures and lifting and support and rigging training; hot work and electrical and confined space operation training and permits; personal protection and emergency response and drills; requirements for the disposal and reporting of waste oil and grime and waste and noise; and requirements for identifying and reporting equipment and site hazards.

Checklist point notes | U.S. O*NET places 49-3042.00 (Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanics) in Job Zone Three (medium preparation required), with an SVP range of 6.0 to less than 7.0 (SVP 6.0 to < 7.0); the education section shows 55% requiring a post-secondary certificate, 30% a high school diploma or equivalent, and 8% some college courses but no degree (the page does not account for the remaining 7%); this occupation is marked Bright Outlook; in the United States preparation for this occupation is usually vocational school training or on-the-job experience or an associate degree with one to two years of training.

03 Education and training and apprenticeship and qualification requirements | Check whether vocational school training or an associate degree or relevant on-the-job experience is required (that page's Job Zone Three (medium preparation required) and SVP 6.0 to less than 7.0 (SVP 6.0 to < 7.0)); whether a registered apprenticeship or mentor-based training is provided; whether welding and lifting and electrical and confined space qualifications or in-house enterprise training and assessment are required; and whether the training and assessment cover diagnosis and disassembly and repair and overhaul and testing and safety and emergency response.

Checklist point notes | This occupation is mainly repair and operation and inspection and decision making (repairing and maintaining mechanical equipment 88 and operating vehicles 86 and inspecting equipment 85 and making decisions and solving problems 83 are the highest activities; exposure to hazardous equipment and oil and noise and confined spaces is common, consequences of error are serious, and there are downtime and schedule constraints), so the site environment and physical and safety tolerance must be included in the check.

04 Pay, working hours, and employment contract scope | Check the composition of the offered pay (base wage, overtime and field and emergency service and night shift allowances, performance and piece rate and travel allowances, differences by enterprise type and region, social insurance and housing fund and labor protection and tools and vehicle arrangements), working hours and scheduling and travel and standby arrangements, contract term and probation and termination conditions, and training and qualification and promotion arrangements; the U.S.-scope median and percentiles serve only as market reference and are not equal to the offer of any enterprise or region.

Checklist point notes | The interface relationships with operators and supervisors and projects and suppliers and equipment manufacturers and safety parties determine the boundaries of diagnosis and disposition and acceptance and authorization and responsibility and disclosure, and must be clarified in advance.

05 Interface authority with operators and suppliers and regulators | Check the authority to adjust and modify equipment parameters and settings, the arrangements for applying for and using and reviewing tools and diagnostic equipment and spare parts, the path for diagnosis and repair and testing and acceptance and nonconforming or rework items, and the requirements for handling and externally providing customer and manufacturer technical materials and drawings and data.

Checklist point notes | The traceability and record-keeping requirements for work orders and diagnosis and testing and repair and acceptance and spare parts and anomalies determine quality and responsibility definition, and the specifications for templates and time limits and modification and archiving and authority and retention periods must be clarified in advance (materials involving customer and manufacturer technical materials must also be managed under confidentiality and minimum necessity requirements).

06 Repair and inspection and records and traceability requirements | Check the requirements for repair request and work order records, on-site inspection and diagnosis and test records, disassembly and repair or replacement and overhaul records, assembly and adjustment and subassembly records, performance test and acceptance records, spare parts and inventory records, anomaly and rework and outstanding item records, and work permits and handover and original records and revision trail.

Evidence note | The comparison objects in the table below come from the O*NET occupational classification and public materials, and are used to help distinguish the work content of adjacent occupations and choose a fit; they do not constitute qualification, hiring, or pay conclusions, nor safety, special operations, or legal advice. The wages and employment of each occupation must be checked according to its own occupational code and statistical scope and cannot be applied to one another.

Preface | The following comparison is presented in four columns: "career direction — core work and outputs — key differences — what it suits better". Mobile heavy equipment repair and operation and diesel engine and farm machinery and lifting positions often connect within the same equipment life cycle and construction site, but connection does not mean they are interchangeable; each position differs in subject matter, equipment, qualifications, and responsibility boundaries and must be checked separately.

Key difference: this occupation takes mobile heavy machinery and hydraulic and pneumatic and electrical systems as its subject matter, completing diagnosis and repair and overhaul and testing within the scope of qualifications and job authorization based on mechanical and hydraulic and electrical and diagnostic ability, and is responsible for equipment and personal safety and repair quality; adjacent positions take operation or engines or farm machinery or lifting as their subject matter, with different specialties and authorization.

Apply digital tools to reversible supporting steps: organizing work orders and equipment ledgers, retrieving repair manuals and spare parts, entering diagnostic and test readings; disassembly and repair and safety judgments are governed by mentoring and authorization.

Direct answer | The core risk of this occupation is not "can the equipment be repaired", but four types of failure with heavier consequences: safety and personal failure (hydraulic and pneumatic high pressure, lifting and support, hot work and electrical, confined spaces and mechanical injury); quality and recurrence failure (inadequate diagnosis or repair or assembly leading to a recurring fault and a second downtime); equipment failure (improper disassembly or adjustment causing equipment damage); and record and traceability failure (distorted repair and inspection data making responsibility impossible to define).

entries.answer: The Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanics on this page is the exact occupation O*NET 49-3042.00 (Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanics, Except Engines): diagnose, adjust, repair, or overhaul mobile mechanical, hydraulic, and pneumatic equipment used in construction, logging, and mining, such as cranes, bulldozers, graders, and conveyors. Core tasks include repairing and replacing damaged or worn parts, testing equipment after repair or assembly to ensure proper performance and conformity with manufacturer specifications, operating and inspecting equipment to diagnose defects, reading and understanding operating manuals and drawings and technical diagrams, and disassembling and reassembling equipment using rigging and hand tools. Common job titles include Heavy Equipment Mechanic and Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanic and Field Service Technician.

subject.name: Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanics
subject.summary: Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanics corresponds to the exact occupation O*NET/SOC 49-3042.00 "Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanics, Except Engines": diagnose, adjust, repair, or overhaul mobile mechanical, hydraulic, and pneumatic equipment used in construction, logging, and mining, such as cranes, bulldozers, graders, and conveyors. Core tasks include operating and inspecting equipment to diagnose defects, repairing or replacing damaged or worn parts, disassembling and overhauling and reassembling, reading and understanding materials according to manuals and drawings, and testing equipment to ensure it meets manufacturer specifications; common job titles include Heavy Equipment Mechanic and Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanic and Field Service Technician and Heavy Equipment Technician. Official scope text: Diagnose, adjust, repair, or overhaul mobile mechanical, hydraulic, and pneumatic equipment, such as cranes, bulldozers, graders, and conveyors, used in construction, logging, and mining. Scope note: the U.S. wage and employment and industry data presented by O*NET on the 49-3042.00 page are not marked as taken from a parent or adjacent occupation, and this page labels them faithfully according to this occupation's (49-3042.00) own scope; this occupation is Job Zone Three (medium preparation required) (6.0 to less than 7.0 (SVP 6.0 to < 7.0)), with 2024—2034 growth of Faster than average (5% to 6%) and marked Bright Outlook.
